extracted.intended_audience: students, playwrights, literary critics, and theorists of comedy/humor
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic theory of what makes situations and words comic, focusing on mechanisms (repetition, inversion, interference) and how language itself produces comic effects. Drawn from a literary/philosophical essay aimed at explaining and illustrating comedic devices in theatre and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comique as mechanization / rigidity
rubrics_metrics.description: «Le comique est ce côté de la personne par lequel elle ressemble à une chose...le mécanisme pur et simple, l'automatisme, enfin le mouvement sans la vie.» The comic arises when living beings are perceived as mechanical, rigid, or automatic — a movement without life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter functions as social correction of an individual or collective imperfection: showing someone as a mechanism exposes an imperfection that invites correction. Use imagery or behaviour that suggests automatism, stiffness, or detachable parts to elicit this comic reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (La répétition)
rubrics_metrics.description: «Il s’agit...d’une situation...qui revient telle quelle à plusieurs reprises, tranchant ainsi sur le cours changeant de la vie.» Repeating a full situation (not just a word) creates comic effect by contrasting life's expected irreversibility with an identical recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More complex repeated scenes and more natural lead-ins increase comedy; balance complexity and naturalness (authorial skill reconciling the two). Examples: recurring three-part effects in Molière (L'École des Femmes, George Dandin) and vaudeville devices that carry a group of characters through different milieus to revive the same misadventure. Repetition can occur between different character groups (masters/domestics) or across acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (L'inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: «Faire que la situation se retourne et que les rôles soient intervertis.» Comedy arises when roles or situations are reversed — the persecutor becomes the persecuted, the dupe duper becomes the duped, or an expected hierarchy is turned upside-down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion can be shown directly or only implied (audience imagines the counterpart). Use role-reversal scenes (e.g., double rescues), the 'voleur volé' theme, or put characters into the traps they set. Recognize that repeated comic scenes can become 'categories' (stock comic types) that trigger laughter by association.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference of series (L'interférence des séries)
rubrics_metrics.description: «Une situation est toujours comique quand elle appartient en même temps à deux séries d'événements absolument indépendantes, et qu'elle peut s'interpréter à la fois dans deux sens tout différents.» The quiproquo is a particular case: two independent event-series intersect so that actions have legitimate meaning in each series, producing equivocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the audience aware of both independent series while keeping characters aware only of one, creating oscillation between false and true judgments. Create near-breaks and reconciliations to sustain tension: continuously threaten dissociation between series, then re-establish coincidence. Examples: quiproquos, transposition of past/modern events (Daudet), Labiche's cross-series interferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life as artistic aim
rubrics_metrics.description: «On prendra un système d'actions et de relations, et on le répétera tel quel, ou on le retournera...ou on le transportera en bloc dans un autre système...» The theatrical objective is to obtain a 'mechanisation' of life — treating living actions as repeatable, reversible, and interchangeable mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition, inversion, or transport of an action-system into a mismatched milieu to expose life's automatism. Vaudeville exaggerates this to a puppet-like artifice; distinguish this light game from deeper comédie de caractère which roots comedy in more permanent personality features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: comic of events vs comic of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Vaudeville (comic of events) emphasizes mechanical, detachable incidents and is conventionally artificial and light; comédie de caractère (comic of character) grows from deeper, more stable personal dispositions and is more 'classical' and rooted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to foreground external contrivances (repeatable, transportable incidents) or internal dispositions (character forces whose consistent directions naturally produce repetition). Classical comedy derives repetition from character consistency; contemporary vaudeville often works on the spectator's mind instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience preparation vs character-driven plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods to make an extraordinary coincidence acceptable: (1) prepare the spectator gradually so the coincidence is accepted; (2) make the repetition/nonsense arise from the characters' dispositions so it seems natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporary authors often manipulate spectator expectations directly (foreshadowing, staging); classical authors build coincidences from consistent character motivations. Choose strategy depending on tone (artificial vs organic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comique de mots: language that creates the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish comique que le langage exprime (language expressing pre-existing comic) from comique que le langage crée (language itself produces incomparably original comic effects — often untranslatable and due to phrase structure/word choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To create comic with words, exploit the shape, clichés, idioms, metaphors and syntactic possibilities of language itself rather than merely reporting amusing events. Many word-based effects depend on language-specific stock phrases and are thus hard to translate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic phrase + inserted absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: «On obtiendra toujours un mot comique en insérant une idée absurde dans un moule de phrase consacré.» Inserting an absurdity into a clichéd automatic phrase reveals the speaker's mechanical utterance and produces comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-known stock endings or idioms, then place an incongruous or absurd element inside to expose the automatism. Examples: M. Prudhomme's lines; the example 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie' – the absurdity awakens laughter by showing the phrase spoken mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalization / materialization of metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: «On obtient un effet comique toutes les fois qu'on affecte d'entendre une expression au propre, alors qu'elle était employée au figuré.» Making a metaphor literal or focusing on the physicality of a figurative phrase produces comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select common metaphors or symbolic phrases and force a concrete interpretation (e.g., 'Tous les arts sont sœurs' vs 'Tous les arts sont cousins'); amplified concreteness yields comic effect. Use concrete vocabulary from other domains (sport, trade) to materialize an abstract phrase for humorous effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation-comic laws applied to language (repetition, inversion, interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: «Ces trois lois...prendront la forme suivante...»: a sentence becomes comic if it can be (a) repeated/transported into another tone/milieu, (b) inverted to yield another sense, or (c) made to carry two independent systems of ideas simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same three theatrical procedures to series of words/ideas: repeat phrases in new tones, invert grammatical roles to create a new sense, or superpose two semantic systems in one sentence. Priority: interference (double-meaning superposition) is richest; inversion is easiest but less valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion of sentence structure for wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Turning a sentence inside-out (subject↔object, etc.) can yield a witty or comic retort by forcing a new, unexpected sense from familiar phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common among practiced wits: attempt to reverse syntactic roles to refute or mock an idea. Example: 'Pourquoi jetez-vous vos pipes sur ma terrasse?' → 'Pourquoi mettez‑vous votre terrasse sous mes pipes ?' Use sparingly — the essay judges inversion the least interesting of the three linguistic transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference of two idea-systems within one phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: «Il y a bien des moyens...de donner à la même phrase deux significations indépendantes qui se superposent.» Creating a superposition of two independent meanings in one expression produces sustained amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft sentences that legitimately read in two independent ways (semantic layering), so the listener oscillates or perceives both senses. This is a plentiful source of comic effects; techniques include double metaphors, emblem-development taken materially, and juxtaposing idioms with literal senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock comic categories and associative resonance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a scene or device is often repeated it becomes a 'catégorie' or model; new scenes that resemble it will evoke the comic by associative resonance even if not comic by themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or invoke known comic types (e.g., 'voleur volé', quiproquo) to trigger audience recognition and laughter by association. Short references or echoes to such types can make otherwise neutral incidents funny through their resonances.
